title: StateFlow vs LiveData & One-Off Events
scopeHtml: Scope: how StateFlow differs from LiveData (lifecycle, threading, conflation, interop), migrating LiveData to Flow, and the one-off event debate (SharedFlow vs Channel vs events-as-state, current Google guidance). StateFlow/SharedFlow internals belong to the F2a chunk; stateIn/repeatOnLifecycle depth belongs to F5.

notes.title: StateFlow versus LiveData overview
notes.html:
The idea. Both hold "the current value of the screen" and tell the UI when it changes. LiveData is the older Android-only tool with built-in lifecycle smarts. StateFlow is the Kotlin-coroutines tool: pure Kotlin, works anywhere, has operators, but needs you to wire up lifecycle yourself.

LiveData StateFlow
Library AndroidX lifecycle-livedata kotlinx.coroutines (platform independent)
Initial value optional (can be empty) mandatory
Reading now liveData.value (nullable) stateFlow.value (non-null if T is)
Lifecycle-aware built in (STARTED+ delivers) no, use repeatOnLifecycle / collectAsStateWithLifecycle
Equality dedupe no (setValue always notifies) yes (equals)
Threads setValue main only, postValue any .value any thread
Operators few (map, switchMap, distinctUntilChanged) the full Flow operator set
Java usage easy awkward
Testing needs InstantTaskExecutorRule plain coroutines test

Initial value and reading state. A StateFlow's .value is always available, so non-UI code (a repository, a ViewModel function) can simply read the current state to decide an action: if (state.value.isLoading) return. With LiveData .value can be null before first set, forcing !! or ?.. This is a major reason Google's guidance moved to StateFlow for new Kotlin code, together with its dedupe and testability.

Real examples. Older apps (early Gmail/Google Maps-style codebases, many Paytm/Flipkart screens written 2018-2020) are LiveData + Data Binding; new Compose screens (Now in Android) use StateFlow. Many large apps run both during a multi-year migration.

Everyday picture. LiveData is a smart doorbell that only rings when you are home; StateFlow is a plain bell that rings always, and you must remember to switch it off when you leave.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "StateFlow is lifecycle-aware": it is not.
  • Forgetting StateFlow requires an initial value and LiveData does not.
  • Thinking LiveData.value is non-null.

notes.title: Lifecycle awareness and repeatOnLifecycle
notes.html:
The idea. A screen in the background should not keep doing work and must not touch views that no longer exist. LiveData stops delivering automatically when the screen is not at least STARTED. A raw lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect {...} } does not: it keeps collecting while the app is in the background and the upstream (a database query, a location listener) keeps running: a wasted-battery bug.

Mechanism. The fix is repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED): it launches the block when the lifecycle reaches STARTED and cancels it when the lifecycle drops below STARTED, restarting on the next STARTED. Compose's collectAsStateWithLifecycle() does the same thing. For several flows, launch them inside one repeatOnLifecycle block.

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        vm.state.collect { render(it) }
    }
}

Upstream lifetime and leaks. Cancelling the collector is only half the story: whether the upstream stops depends on how the flow is shared. stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, ...) keeps the upstream running forever; WhileSubscribed(5_000) stops it 5 seconds after the last collector leaves (the 5 s is chosen to survive configuration changes like rotation without restarting upstream, and it matches the ANR threshold on Android, a widely quoted number from Google). Lazily starts at first collector and never stops. Common leaks: lifecycleScope.launch { collect } in a Fragment using lifecycleScope of the Fragment instead of viewLifecycleOwner (collector outlives the view, holds the binding: LeakCanary reports the Fragment view leaked); collecting in onCreate without repeatOnLifecycle; a repository singleton holding a MutableSharedFlow collected by a collector capturing an Activity.

Real examples. A Google Maps-style screen with a live location flow: with WhileSubscribed the GPS listener stops when the user backgrounds the app; with Eagerly the GPS drains battery until the process dies. Play Console "excessive wakeups/background location" warnings are the production symptom.

Everyday picture. A shop that opens its tills when customers enter (STARTED) and shuts them when the last one leaves; with Eagerly the lights and AC run all night.

Common interview traps.

  • Using lifecycleScope.launch { collect } and thinking it is lifecycle-aware (it only cancels at DESTROYED).
  • Using the Fragment's lifecycleScope instead of viewLifecycleOwner.
  • Using launchWhenStarted (deprecated): it only pauses, the upstream still runs.
  • Forgetting that WhileSubscribed(5000) is what actually stops the upstream.

notes.title: Threading: setValue, postValue and StateFlow
notes.html:
The idea. LiveData has two doors: setValue for the main thread and postValue for any thread. StateFlow has one door that works from any thread.

Mechanism. LiveData.setValue must be called on the main thread (it asserts, throwing IllegalStateException: Cannot invoke setValue on a background thread). postValue stores the value in a field and posts one Runnable to the main thread; if you call postValue several times before the main thread runs, only the last value is delivered (lost updates). postValue(a); setValue(b) can even deliver in a surprising order, b then a. MutableStateFlow.value = x is thread-safe via atomics, conflates the same way (latest wins), and notifies collectors on whatever dispatcher they collect on. Hence StateFlow is simpler: no "which thread am I on" worry.

// LiveData: lost update
repeat(3) { live.postValue(it) }    // UI may only see 2
// StateFlow: UI also may only see the latest, but it is the documented contract
repeat(3) { state.value = it }

Real examples. Background Room or Retrofit callbacks calling postValue from an OkHttp thread were the origin of many "my progress jumped from 0 to 100" or "state missing" bugs; Crashlytics shows IllegalStateException: Cannot invoke setValue on a background thread when someone moved a call into withContext(Dispatchers.IO).

Everyday picture. setValue is handing a note to the manager in person; postValue is dropping notes in an inbox where only the newest is read when the manager returns.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling setValue from a background thread.
  • Believing postValue delivers every value.
  • Assuming StateFlow collectors run on the thread that set the value (they run in the collector's context).

notes.title: Conflation, equality and mutable collections
notes.html:
The idea. LiveData tells the UI on every setValue, even if the value is the same. StateFlow stays silent if the new value equals the old. This changes behaviour on migration.

Mechanism. LiveData: set the same value twice and observers fire twice (that "feature" is why Android devs used it as a crude event channel). StateFlow: equal means no emission. For a data class equality is structural; for a normal class it is identity. A MutableList inside state is the trap: the same list instance mutated in place equals itself, so nothing is emitted.

// BUG: same instance, StateFlow sees no change, RecyclerView does not refresh
val list = _state.value.items as MutableList
list.add(newItem)
_state.value = _state.value.copy(items = list)

// FIX: new immutable list each time
_state.update { it.copy(items = it.items + newItem) }

Use immutable List types, persistentListOf from kotlinx.collections.immutable (also helps Compose stability and skipping), and copy(). In the reverse direction, code ported from LiveData that depended on "set the same value to re-trigger" (e.g. "refresh" button) silently stops working.

Real examples. Instagram-like feed state with items: List<Post>; an in-place add made likes not show until another change. DiffUtil / Compose LazyColumn need distinct list instances to compare.

Everyday picture. Reprinting a menu: if you scribble on the existing copy the manager's "has the menu changed?" check compares the copy to itself and says no; hand over a new printed copy and it notices.

Common interview traps.

  • Mutating a list in state in place.
  • Expecting StateFlow to re-notify on an equal value.
  • Putting a var property inside a state data class.

notes.title: Java and View-system interop
notes.html:
The idea. LiveData is easy from Java and the old View system (Data Binding, observe(owner, observer)). StateFlow needs coroutines, which Java and XML bindings handle poorly.

Mechanism. From Java you cannot call suspend collect easily; you would need FlowLiveDataConversions/asLiveData() (androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-livedata-ktx) or wrapper helpers. Data Binding supports StateFlow in android:text="@{vm.state}" from AGP 7.x/Data Binding 7.x onward (check docs for your AGP version) if you set a lifecycle owner on the binding. For mixed codebases the pragmatic bridge is stateFlow.asLiveData() (uses liveData{} builder; its upstream stays active for 5 s after the last observer disappears, timeoutInMs = 5000) and liveData.asFlow() for the reverse.

Real examples. Big legacy apps (banking/telecom apps with Java modules, SDKs offering Java API) keep LiveData in public APIs and use Flow internally. A library SDK used by Java clients often exposes LiveData or callbacks, not Flow.

Everyday picture. An old plug in a new country: you do not rewire the house, you use an adapter (asLiveData) at the boundary.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying Java can collect a Flow directly.
  • Using asLiveData() and forgetting it buffers/conflates differently than the Flow source.
  • Exposing Flow in a public SDK API without considering Java consumers.

notes.title: Migrating LiveData to Flow
notes.html:
The idea. Migrate from the inside out, one layer at a time, so the app keeps shipping.

Plan that works under live traffic.

  1. Start at the data layer: change Room DAOs and repositories to return Flow<T> (Room supports it natively). Keep ViewModel's public LiveData using repo.flow.asLiveData() so no UI changes yet.
  2. Move the ViewModel to MutableStateFlow with an asStateFlow() public property. In the UI, replace observe with repeatOnLifecycle collection (Fragment) or collectAsStateWithLifecycle (Compose). Do it screen by screen behind the same release train.
  3. Replace MediatorLiveData by combine, switchMap by flatMapLatest, Transformations.map by map.
  4. Replace single-live-event hacks (see event sections) by an explicit mechanism.
  5. Remove asLiveData() bridges at the end.

Behaviour differences to test. Initial value now mandatory (add a Loading state); equal values no longer re-notify; postValue threading rules vanish; lifecycle handling becomes your job (leaks if forgotten); unit tests change from InstantTaskExecutorRule to coroutine test dispatchers; observers previously only ran when STARTED, now they depend on your repeatOnLifecycle. Verify with LeakCanary and a Crashlytics/Firebase staged rollout (e.g. 5% then 25%), watching ANR and crash-free rate.

Real examples. Google's Architecture Samples and Now in Android document this order; large teams (Square, Airbnb, Reddit engineering blogs) describe migrations over several quarters, module by module.

Everyday picture. Replacing the pipes in an occupied building floor by floor, keeping water running at each step.

Common interview traps.

  • Big-bang rewrite of all screens in one release.
  • Forgetting that the same-value re-notify behaviour disappears.
  • Leaving asLiveData() in place forever, hiding double buffering.

notes.title: One-off events and stickiness
notes.html:
The idea. Some things happen once: "show this snackbar", "go to the next screen". They are not state. If you store them in a state holder, they come back (sticky) when the screen is recreated, so the snackbar appears again after rotation or the app navigates twice.

Mechanism. LiveData and StateFlow both replay their latest value to a new observer/collector. After rotation the Fragment is recreated and re-collects, so the last "NavigateToDetail" value is delivered again: the user is pushed forward a second time, or a back-stack gets two copies of the screen (a classic production bug, visible as the user pressing back and landing on a duplicate Details). Same for toast/snackbar: rotating the phone replays "Payment failed" a second time.

Production incident (navigation). After a login success the ViewModel sets navEvent.value = GoHome. User presses Back from Home; the Login Fragment's view is recreated, observer attaches, receives sticky GoHome again and immediately navigates to Home again: the user can never go back. Crashlytics shows nothing (no crash), support tickets say "back button broken". Fix: treat navigation as an event consumed exactly once.

Evolution of fixes. SingleLiveEvent (Google sample; one observer, AtomicBoolean flag; breaks with multiple observers), Event<T> wrapper with getContentIfNotHandled() (consumed on first read; breaks if the first reader is not the one who should act, e.g. a collector that was started but the view was gone), Channel + receiveAsFlow(), SharedFlow(replay=0), and Google's current guidance: model it as state, then clear it after consumption.

Everyday picture. A voicemail that replays itself every time you pick up the phone, versus a one-time doorbell.

Common interview traps.

  • Using StateFlow/LiveData for navigation and not expecting replay.
  • Using Event.getContentIfNotHandled() and being surprised by multiple observers.
  • Thinking SingleLiveEvent is lifecycle-safe with multiple observers.

notes.title: One-off events: options compared and Google's guidance
notes.html:
The idea. There are four ways. Know their failure modes.

Option Delivery when nobody collects Multiple collectors Rotation Verdict
SharedFlow(replay=0) lost all get it lost if gap loses events
SharedFlow(replay=1) replayed to new collector all get it duplicate after rotation sticky bug
Channel(BUFFERED/UNLIMITED) + receiveAsFlow() buffered until collected each event to ONE collector only kept in buffer works for single consumer, can lose in cancel race
Event as state + consumed() callback kept in state state shows once survives if not consumed Google's recommendation

Google guidance. The official Android architecture docs (UI events guidance) say: ViewModel exposes UI state; events that cause UI behavior (navigation, snackbar) should be modelled as state too, with the UI telling the ViewModel when the event is handled so the ViewModel clears it. Rationale: "events are not guaranteed to be delivered" when UI is not collecting, and state is.

data class UiState(val items: List<Item> = emptyList(), val userMessage: String? = null)

fun onMessageShown() { _state.update { it.copy(userMessage = null) } }

// UI
state.userMessage?.let { snackbar(it); vm.onMessageShown() }

Standardizing across a team (design trade-off). Pick one pattern and ship a tiny helper plus a lint rule/code review checklist. Costs of the state approach: more boilerplate, the UI must remember to call onShown(), and idempotence matters if the call is lost. Costs of Channel: single-consumer only, events during no-collector windows buffered (good) but dropped when the receiving coroutine is cancelled at the wrong time. Teams like Google's samples, Slack or Reddit tend to end up with "state + consume" for navigation and snackbars, and Channel for fire-and-forget analytics-like signals. Whatever is chosen, tests assert the event appears exactly once across a configuration change.

Everyday picture. A restaurant order slip clipped on a rail (state) stays until the cook removes it, while shouting across the kitchen (SharedFlow replay 0) is lost if the cook was in the pantry.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "just use SharedFlow" without addressing the gap where no one is collecting.
  • Forgetting that a Channel delivers each event to exactly one collector.
  • Not clearing the event after consumption (state approach), causing replay.
  • Mixing patterns across screens in one codebase.

notes.title: Channel as an event bus: where it loses events
notes.html:
The idea. A Channel is a queue: one side sends, one side receives, items wait. It feels perfect for events, but it has three leak points.

Mechanism. Channel<Event>(Channel.BUFFERED) + val events = channel.receiveAsFlow(); send with channel.send(e) (suspends if full) or trySend. Loss scenarios:

  1. Bounded capacity with trySend. Default BUFFERED is 64 slots; trySend on a full channel returns failure (a closed/failed result) and the event is dropped silently. Use UNLIMITED only when producers are truly low-volume (unbounded memory).
  2. Cancellation race. A collector that receives an element and is then cancelled before processing (e.g. rotation exactly then) has already consumed it: the event is gone. Channel(onUndeliveredElement = { ... }) lets you handle elements that were sent but not delivered, but an element delivered to a cancelled receiver is a known edge.
  3. Multiple collectors. receiveAsFlow() is fan-out: each event goes to only one of several collectors (round-robin-ish), so two screens or a re-collection may "steal" events. consumeAsFlow() can only be collected once and throws IllegalStateException on a second collect.
  4. Unconsumed after the screen is gone. Events buffered while the UI is away are delivered later when it returns, possibly long after they matter (a snackbar for a payment shown minutes later).

Real examples. Navigation events in a ViewModel with Compose's LaunchedEffect(Unit) { vm.events.collect { ... } }: during rotation the effect is cancelled and relaunched; typically ok due to buffering, but a rare event lost mid-processing was reported in Android developer threads (the "Channel events can be lost" discussions) which is why Google recommended state-based events.

Everyday picture. A postbox with one slot reader: letters wait inside, but if two neighbours open it, each takes different letters, and a letter taken by someone who then fainted is gone.

Common interview traps.

  • Using trySend on a bounded Channel and ignoring the result.
  • Using consumeAsFlow() and collecting twice (crash).
  • Assuming a Channel broadcasts to all collectors.
  • Thinking a Channel makes events exactly-once under cancellation.

notes.title: Snackbar events and standardization
notes.html:
The idea. A snackbar is the most common one-off event, and it has its own bugs: it re-shows after rotation, shows twice, or stacks.

Spot-the-bug.

// ViewModel
private val _error = MutableStateFlow<String?>(null)
val error = _error.asStateFlow()
fun load() = viewModelScope.launch { try { repo.get() } catch (e: Exception) { _error.value = e.message } }

// Fragment
vm.error.collect { it?.let { showSnackbar(it) } }   // BUG

Problems: (1) nothing ever resets error to null, so after rotation the collector gets the old message and shows it again; (2) if the same error string happens twice, StateFlow dedupes and the second failure shows nothing (same value, no emission), because the first was never cleared. Fix: onErrorShown() that sets it back to null after showing (and show with a unique id, e.g. data class UiMessage(val id: Long, val text: String), to make repeated identical messages distinct, as Google's "Now in Android" does for messages). In Compose, a SnackbarHostState.showSnackbar called inside LaunchedEffect(state.userMessage) and then onMessageShown().

Real examples. Google's architecture-samples (TODO app) keep userMessage: Int? in state and a snackbarMessageShown() function; many apps wrap messages with ids/timestamps to guarantee distinctness.

Everyday picture. A reminder sticky note on the fridge: if no one takes it down, the next person reads it again.

Common interview traps.

  • Never resetting the message after showing it.
  • Same message twice being swallowed by StateFlow's dedupe.
  • Showing a snackbar from a background collector with no active UI.
  • Using a Toast from a ViewModel directly (leaks Context).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• StateFlow: mandatory initial value, .value readable anywhere, dedupes by equals, no lifecycle awareness; LiveData: optional value, lifecycle-aware, re-notifies on same value, easy from Java/Data Binding.
  • Use repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) / collectAsStateWithLifecycle and WhileSubscribed(5000) so collection and upstream stop in the background; collect with viewLifecycleOwner in Fragments.
  • setValue is main thread only; postValue can coalesce updates; StateFlow value writes are thread-safe.
  • Never mutate collections in state; copy with update { it.copy(...) }.
  • Migrate data layer first, then ViewModels, then UI, with bridges asLiveData() / asFlow() and a staged rollout.
  • One-off events: StateFlow/LiveData/replay-1 are sticky (rotation bugs); replay-0 SharedFlow loses events; Channel is single-consumer with cancellation and capacity edges; Google recommends modelling events as state and clearing them after consumption.
  • Snackbars and navigation need a consume step, distinct message ids and a team-wide standard.

questions.promptHtml: What are the main differences between LiveData and StateFlow, and why did Google move its guidance toward StateFlow for ViewModel state?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every Android codebase has both. They want to know if you understand the trade, not just "StateFlow is newer".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Both are observable state holders that replay the latest value to new observers. LiveData is lifecycle-aware by itself and Android-only, so it stops delivering when the UI is not started. StateFlow is a plain Kotlin coroutines type: it needs an initial value, has .value readable from any thread, de-duplicates equal values, works with all Flow operators, and runs in pure-Kotlin and multiplatform code. The price is that lifecycle awareness is no longer free: I must collect with repeatOnLifecycle or collectAsStateWithLifecycle."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect LiveData StateFlow
Platform Android (androidx.lifecycle) Kotlin / KMP (kotlinx.coroutines)
Initial value Optional (MutableLiveData() has none) Mandatory
Reading value getValue() nullable, T? .value non-null T
Lifecycle awareness Built in: delivers only while observer is STARTED/RESUMED, auto-removes at DESTROYED None: collector runs until its coroutine is cancelled
Threads setValue main only; postValue any thread .value = any thread, update {} CAS
Equal values Always dispatched (no dedupe) Skipped if old == new (equals)
Rapid updates postValue coalesces; setValue each dispatched Conflated: slow collector sees only the latest
Operators map, switchMap, MediatorLiveData Whole Flow operator set
Completion/errors None Never completes; exception handling is your job
Testing Needs InstantTaskExecutorRule runTest + Turbine, no Android deps

Why the guidance moved: (1) the data layer (Room, DataStore, Retrofit wrappers) is already Flow/suspend, so LiveData forces conversions at the ViewModel boundary; (2) LiveData lives in the UI-layer library, so it should not leak into domain/data modules; (3) operator richness (combine, debounce, flatMapLatest); (4) Compose and KMP use Flow; (5) LiveData is not deprecated, but new code is steered to StateFlow.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class ProfileViewModel(repo: ProfileRepo) : ViewModel() {
    val uiState: StateFlow<ProfileUiState> = repo.observeProfile()
        .map { ProfileUiState.Content(it) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), ProfileUiState.Loading)
}

// Fragment
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.uiState.collect(::render)
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "StateFlow replaces LiveData completely": LiveData is still fine, supported, and simpler in a Views-only app that is not migrating.
  • Collecting StateFlow with plain lifecycleScope.launch { collect }: it keeps running while in background (see F5 chunk).
  • Thinking StateFlow is lifecycle-aware because it is "state".

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is LiveData deprecated? → No. Still maintained; recommended for new code is Flow in lower layers and StateFlow/collectAsStateWithLifecycle in UI.
  2. Can you use StateFlow from Java? → Awkwardly. Collection needs coroutines; convert with asLiveData() or expose a bridge. Java screens stay on LiveData.
  3. What do you lose moving to StateFlow? → Automatic lifecycle handling, Transformations convenience, data-binding setLifecycleOwner out of the box (data binding does support StateFlow since AGP 7+/ Data Binding 7, with lifecycle owner set), and you gain thread-safety, dedupe, operators.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists "StateFlow needs initial value, LiveData is lifecycle-aware". Senior frames it as layering: Flow in data/domain, StateFlow at the ViewModel boundary, lifecycle handled at the collection site, and names the semantic differences (dedupe, conflation, completion) that cause behavior changes during migration.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team migrated a settings screen; a toggle "refresh" that relied on LiveData re-dispatching equal values silently stopped refreshing because StateFlow deduplicated equal state.

questions.promptHtml: LiveData can be empty but StateFlow must have an initial value. How does that change how you model "not loaded yet", and what does .value give you vs liveData.value?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you model loading explicitly instead of relying on null/absence.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A MutableLiveData() with no value does not notify observers until someone sets one, and getValue() returns null, so 'no value yet' is implicit. StateFlow can never be empty, so I make loading an explicit state in a sealed UiState: Loading, Content, Error. stateFlow.value is non-null and thread-safe to read, but reading it is a snapshot, not a subscription."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• LiveData with no value: observers attach, nothing is delivered (internally mVersion == START_VERSION (-1), so the observer's mLastVersion >= mVersion check blocks delivery). A UI waiting for it renders nothing, which looks like a blank screen.
  • LiveData<T>.getValue() returns T? in Kotlin (platform type issues in older versions; lifecycle 2.6+ made T? explicit on getValue()). Callers null-check or crash.
  • StateFlow always has a value, so first collection emits immediately. The initial value often is Loading - which means the UI draws a spinner on first frame instead of nothing.
  • Pitfall: using null as initial for StateFlow<User?> conflates "loading" with "logged out".
  • .value is read-only on StateFlow, read/write on MutableStateFlow. Never use .value as if it were the up-to-date result of an async operation; for read-modify-write use update {}.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
sealed interface UserUiState {
    data object Loading : UserUiState
    data class Content(val user: User) : UserUiState
    data class Error(val message: String) : UserUiState
}

private val _state = MutableStateFlow<UserUiState>(UserUiState.Loading)
val state: StateFlow<UserUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• MutableStateFlow<User?>(null) meaning three things at once.
  • _state.value = _state.value.copy(...) from multiple coroutines (lost update); use update.
  • Assuming the initial value is "free": it is rendered, so it must be a valid UI.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if I truly do not have an initial value yet? → Use a Loading sealed state; or stateIn with a suspending overload (stateIn(scope) suspends until first emission) in non-UI code; avoid it in ViewModel init since it blocks property init.
  2. Does the first value always get delivered to a collector? → Yes, a new StateFlow collector always receives the current value first.
  3. What does MutableLiveData(initial) do differently from MutableLiveData()? → The constructor with a value sets mVersion = 0, so new observers receive it (sticky).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "StateFlow needs an initial value". Senior: "That forces me to make absence an explicit state; I avoid nullable-as-state and I use update instead of read-then-write on .value."

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "blank screen on first launch" bug traced to LiveData never set on a path where the repo returned empty; the fix was an explicit Empty state, which StateFlow naturally encouraged.

questions.promptHtml: LiveData is lifecycle-aware; StateFlow is not. What exactly does LiveData do at each lifecycle transition, and how do you get equivalent behavior with StateFlow?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The most common real-world regression in LiveData-to-Flow migrations is lost lifecycle handling.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LiveData wraps each observer in a LifecycleBoundObserver. It only delivers when the owner is at least STARTED, parks the latest value while stopped, redelivers it on restart if it changed, and removes the observer at DESTROYED. StateFlow has none of that: the collector runs until its coroutine is cancelled. To match it I collect inside repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED), which cancels the collection at STOPPED and relaunches at STARTED. In Compose I use collectAsStateWithLifecycle()."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LiveData state machine per observer:

owner state:   INITIALIZED/CREATED  --> STARTED/RESUMED --> CREATED (stop) --> DESTROYED
observer:      inactive (no delivery)   active (delivers)     inactive (holds latest)  removed
on activation: if observer.lastVersion < liveData.version -> deliver latest
  • onActive()/onInactive() hooks fire when the first active observer appears / last leaves; that's how liveData {} and asLiveData() start and stop upstream (with a 5 s timeout default).
  • StateFlow: the collect loop is just a coroutine. If you start it with lifecycleScope.launch { flow.collect {...} }, it runs from the call point until the scope's lifecycle is DESTROYED, including while the app is in the background. Consequences: UI updates on a stopped Fragment (dialogs → IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState), wasted work, and with SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed the upstream never stops.
  • repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) launches the block in a new child coroutine every time the state reaches STARTED and cancels it when it falls below. Because StateFlow replays the latest value, restart behaves like LiveData's redelivery - but it redelivers even if the value is unchanged, while LiveData redelivers only if the version changed. Idempotent render functions make that harmless.
  • Fragment: use viewLifecycleOwner, not the Fragment's own lifecycle, else collectors from the old view leak across view recreation.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fragment, lifecycle-runtime-ktx 2.4+
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        launch { viewModel.uiState.collect(::render) }
        launch { viewModel.title.collect(binding.toolbar::setTitle) }
    }
}

// Compose, lifecycle-runtime-compose 2.6+
val state by viewModel.uiState.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling collect twice sequentially in one repeatOnLifecycle block: the first never returns, second never starts. Use separate launch.
  • launchWhenStarted: only pauses, doesn't cancel, so the upstream keeps producing. Deprecated.
  • Using lifecycleScope of the Fragment rather than viewLifecycleOwner.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does the redelivery difference matter? → Yes: a non-idempotent render (e.g. starting an animation, a toast) will fire again on every restart. Render must be a pure function of state.
  2. How does flowWithLifecycle compare? → It is a single-flow operator built on repeatOnLifecycle; good for one flow, but with several flows use a single repeatOnLifecycle.
  3. How do LiveData observers behave when the Fragment view is destroyed but the Fragment stays on the back stack? → Observers registered with viewLifecycleOwner are removed with the view; with this they leak and observe stale views.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "use repeatOnLifecycle". Senior also names the redelivery-on-restart difference, the WhileSubscribed upstream-stop link, and the viewLifecycleOwner rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: After a migration, a Fragment collected in lifecycleScope.launch and showed a dialog from a background state: crash rate spiked on "state saved" IllegalStateException.

questions.promptHtml: Explain setValue vs postValue on MutableLiveData, the value-loss problem with postValue, and how StateFlow's threading model compares.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Classic gotcha; shows whether you understand main-thread dispatch and conflation.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "setValue must run on the main thread and dispatches synchronously to active observers. postValue can run on any thread: it stores the value in a field and posts one Runnable to the main thread; if you call postValue several times before that Runnable runs, only the last value is delivered. So postValue is lossy and also asynchronous: reading .value right after postValue returns the old value. StateFlow's .value = is safe from any thread, doesn't hop to main, and conflates by design; delivery thread is the collector's dispatcher."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• LiveData.setValue: assertMainThread("setValue") throws IllegalStateException: Cannot invoke setValue on a background thread. Increments mVersion, calls dispatchingValue.
  • LiveData.postValue: synchronized; writes mPendingData; only if it was NOT_SET does it call ArchTaskExecutor.getInstance().postToMainThread(mPostValueRunnable). The Runnable swaps mPendingData and calls setValue. So 5 posts from a worker before main runs -> 1 delivery with the 5th value.
  • Interaction bug: postValue(a); setValue(b) on main: setValue(b) runs immediately, then the pending runnable runs and sets a last, so order is inverted.
  • StateFlow: CAS update; every collector's own coroutine gets the latest; collector context chooses thread (Dispatchers.Main in UI). No main requirement for writers. Because collection happens on collector context, UI-thread safety comes from collect being in a main-confined scope.
  • Loss is deliberate in both, but StateFlow's loss is "intermediate states", usually fine for state, fatal for events.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// LiveData: observer sees only 3, not 1,2 (if main thread is slow to run the runnable)
withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    live.postValue(1); live.postValue(2); live.postValue(3)
}
// StateFlow: any thread, no main hop; atomic read-modify-write
_state.update { it.copy(count = it.count + 1) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using postValue for a sequence of events (progress steps, one-off messages).
  • Reading liveData.value after postValue and expecting the new value.
  • Calling setValue from Dispatchers.Default in a viewModelScope.launch(Dispatchers.Default).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. In a viewModelScope.launch {} (Main.immediate), setValue or postValue? → setValue/.value= is fine; viewModelScope uses Dispatchers.Main.immediate, so it already runs on main.
  2. Does StateFlow guarantee collectors see each value? → No, conflated; collectors may skip. Also equal values are skipped.
  3. How to get exact delivery of every change? → Not StateFlow; use SharedFlow with buffer, a Channel, or model changes as a list/log in state.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior can state that postValue coalesces via mPendingData and the order inversion with mixed setValue/postValue, and ties it to why StateFlow's conflation is acceptable for state but not events.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A download progress bar "jumping" and a final COMPLETE state overwritten by a late postValue(PROGRESS_99) from another thread.

questions.promptHtml: Both LiveData and StateFlow are said to hold "the latest value". How do equality checks and conflation differ between them, and when does that change app behavior?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests precision on dedupe, a top migration source of "UI stopped updating".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "StateFlow compares new vs old with equals and doesn't emit if equal; it's also conflated, so a slow collector only sees the latest value. LiveData has no equality check: setValue(x) twice dispatches twice. postValue coalesces between main-thread runs. So if a feature relied on re-setting the same value to re-trigger the UI, it breaks with StateFlow. And with StateFlow, mutating an object in place and re-assigning the same reference never emits."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• MutableStateFlow.value = x: updateState compares oldState == newState (structural equality via equals, with null sentinel handling). Equal -> no-op, no collector wake-up.
  • Data class equals compares all primary-constructor properties, so a changed copy() with the same content is equal and is skipped - correct. A class without equals override uses reference equality - every new instance emits even if "same".
  • Conflation: StateFlow has a single slot; each collector reads the slot when it resumes. Two quick writes while the collector is busy -> collector sees latest only.
  • LiveData: setValue increments version and dispatches to every active observer, no matter the value. Good for "force refresh", bad for wasted renders.
  • In practice: dedupe is usually a feature (skip redundant diffing/rendering); conflation is wrong for events (consecutive identical events must both fire).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
val s = MutableStateFlow(0)
s.value = 0              // no emission: 0 == 0
data class Msg(val text: String)
val e = MutableStateFlow<Msg?>(null)
e.value = Msg("saved")   // emits
e.value = Msg("saved")   // NOT emitted: data class equal -> second "saved" toast lost

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using StateFlow<String?> for one-off messages: second identical message never shows.
  • Mutable properties in a data class body (not constructor) are ignored by equals.
  • Believing StateFlow dedupe breaks distinctUntilChanged - it's redundant there.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How to force a re-emit of an equal value? → Wrap with a unique id/counter in state, or use events-as-state with a consumed flag; do not hack with null then value.
  2. Does stateIn dedupe too? → Yes, the resulting StateFlow dedupes.
  3. What about List state? → List.equals compares elements, so a new list with the same elements is equal and a mutated same list instance is identical - see the mutable-list scenario.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior links dedupe to correctness of event modelling and to equals quality on UiState classes (including lists, lambdas, and arrays in state).

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: "Retry" button needed to reload but the error state was identical to the previous one, so the StateFlow didn't emit and the UI looked frozen.

questions.promptHtml: Your app has Java screens, data binding layouts, and a ViewModel exposing StateFlow. How do you make that work, and what are the limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks pragmatism: real apps are mixed, and migrations are gradual.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Java can't consume suspending or coroutine-scoped APIs cleanly, so for Java screens I expose LiveData via flow.asLiveData() at the ViewModel edge, or keep LiveData for those screens. For Kotlin Fragments with ViewBinding I collect in repeatOnLifecycle. Data binding supports StateFlow directly when I set binding.lifecycleOwner = viewLifecycleOwner, with AGP 7+; otherwise I bridge with asLiveData()."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Flow.asLiveData(context = EmptyCoroutineContext, timeoutInMs = 5000) (lifecycle-livedata-ktx; merged into lifecycle-livedata in 2.6): creates a CoroutineLiveData that collects the flow when the LiveData becomes active and cancels collection 5 s after it goes inactive, surviving config changes. Value is set via setValue on Dispatchers.Main.immediate.
  • LiveData.asFlow() goes the other way: collects through an observer on main; conflates (uses a Channel(CONFLATED)) so it can lose intermediate values.
  • Java can technically call StateFlow.getValue() for snapshot reads, but collecting needs a Kotlin helper.
  • Data binding: android:text="@{vm.title}" works with StateFlow<String> since Data Binding 7.0; requires lifecycle owner set, else updates are not observed.
  • Both ways mean one source of truth in the ViewModel and an adapter at the edge. Do not hold both a MutableLiveData and a MutableStateFlow for the same data.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class LegacyVm(repo: Repo) : ViewModel() {
    private val state: StateFlow<UiState> = repo.observe()
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), UiState.Loading)
    val stateLive: LiveData<UiState> = state.asLiveData()   // for Java/data binding screens
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Two parallel sources (LiveData + StateFlow) drifting out of sync.
  • Forgetting binding.lifecycleOwner so StateFlow/LiveData bindings silently do nothing.
  • asLiveData() called in a getter: creates a new LiveData (and collection) per call.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the 5 s in asLiveData do? → Keeps the upstream alive through config changes; same idea as WhileSubscribed(5000).
  2. Can Java collect a Flow? → Not nicely; write a Kotlin wrapper using a callback, or convert to LiveData/RxJava.
  3. Why would you not migrate Java screens? → Cost/benefit: they are stable; the conversion edge isolates them until they are rewritten.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior names the adapters, the 5 s timeout and its purpose, the single-source rule, and that asFlow() conflates.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team doing a "big bang" Flow migration spent two sprints; adapters at the edge would have let them ship per screen.

questions.promptHtml: How would you migrate a 200-screen app from LiveData to Flow without a big-bang rewrite? What are the semantic traps?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests migration planning plus knowledge of behavioral differences.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Bottom-up, in the layers that already speak coroutines: Room and repositories return Flow, domain/use-cases use Flow, and the ViewModel exposes StateFlow. At the ViewModel edge, asLiveData() keeps unmigrated screens working. Then I migrate screens one at a time to repeatOnLifecycle/collectAsStateWithLifecycle. The traps: dedupe, no lifecycle awareness, MediatorLiveData and switchMap replacements, and events modelled as LiveData."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Mapping:

LiveData Flow replacement Gotcha
MutableLiveData MutableStateFlow (state) initial value, dedupe
map Flow.map none
switchMap flatMapLatest same cancel-previous semantic
MediatorLiveData of 2+ sources combine(a, b) {} combine waits for all sources to emit once; Mediator doesn't
distinctUntilChanged automatic on StateFlow
liveData { emit } flow {} + stateIn stateIn sharing strategy needs choosing
Transformations.map on UI thread map on collector's dispatcher use flowOn for heavy work
SingleLiveEvent events-as-state, see Q541

Steps:

  1. Freeze new LiveData in the data layer; lint/Detekt rule for new MutableLiveData in repositories.
  2. Data layer: expose Flow, keep temporary LiveData wrappers via asLiveData only at ViewModels.
  3. ViewModel: replace internal MutableLiveData with MutableStateFlow/stateIn; define UiState.
  4. UI: swap observers with repeatOnLifecycle helper (one shared extension to avoid per-screen mistakes).
  5. Remove adapters when no consumers. Traps: tests (remove InstantTaskExecutorRule need; use runTest), observeForever leaks that become eternal collectors, data-binding.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Before
val items: LiveData<List<Item>> = filter.switchMap { repo.items(it).asLiveData() }
// After
val items: StateFlow<List<Item>> = filter
    .flatMapLatest { repo.items(it) }
    .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), emptyList())

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• combine replacing MediatorLiveData that had one source without an initial value: the UI never renders until all sources emit.
  • Starting upstream eagerly with SharingStarted.Eagerly by default and burning battery.
  • Converting everything in one PR; unreviewable.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if a screen needs both? → One source of truth; adapt with asLiveData() at the edge.
  2. How do you test equivalence? → Turbine on the StateFlow; and screenshot/Espresso test for the screen before/after.
  3. Is it worth it for a stable app? → Only where the data layer is Flow already or the screen is being touched; otherwise leave it.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior gives layered order, an operator mapping, semantic differences, and a "stop adding LiveData" guardrail with metrics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A migration of a MediatorLiveData combining 3 sources to combine left the screen blank for users whose third source (a cached promo) was slow; fixed by seeding with onStart { emit(default) }.

questions.promptHtml: Why did the "SingleLiveEvent" pattern exist, why is it considered broken, and what is the underlying problem all event-modelling approaches must solve?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The one-off event debate is the most common senior architecture discussion on Android; they want the reasoning, not a library name.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "LiveData and StateFlow are both sticky: a new observer immediately gets the last value. That's right for state and wrong for events: after rotation the Fragment re-observes and replays 'navigate to details' or 'show error' again. SingleLiveEvent used an AtomicBoolean to hand the value to one observer once. It breaks with multiple observers (only one gets it), loses events when no observer is active, and the pending-flag is not tied to the actual UI consuming it. The root problem is that an event has a producer lifetime (ViewModel) longer than the consumer lifetime (view), so delivery must be decoupled from observation."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two properties conflict:

  1. At-most-once: don't replay after rotation or re-subscription.
  2. At-least-once: don't drop when the UI is not collecting (background, between view recreation). You can't get exactly-once for free across a non-durable producer/consumer. Each approach picks a compromise:
LiveData.setValue(event)      -> sticky: replays on re-observe          (duplicates)
SingleLiveEvent (flag)        -> one observer once; lost if inactive    (loss, multi-observer bug)
SharedFlow(replay=0)          -> dropped if no collector at emit time   (loss)
SharedFlow(replay=1)          -> replays on rotation                    (duplicates)
Channel(BUFFERED).receiveAsFlow -> buffered, one consumer, mostly OK    (loss on cancel mid-handling, 1 consumer)
Events as state + ack         -> kept until UI says "handled"           (at-least-once, UI must ack)

SingleLiveEvent code (from the old architecture-samples):

class SingleLiveEvent<T> : MutableLiveData<T>() {
    private val pending = AtomicBoolean(false)
    override fun observe(owner: LifecycleOwner, observer: Observer<in T>) {
        super.observe(owner) { t -> if (pending.compareAndSet(true, false)) observer.onChanged(t) }
    }
    override fun setValue(t: T?) { pending.set(true); super.setValue(t) }
}

Failure modes: two observers -> only the first to run consumes it; event set while inactive then the view recreated and observer is attached -> OK, but if the first observer is a stale old view it consumes it (observer from the destroyed view are removed, so mostly OK); postValue coalescing drops events; also nothing stops the UI from crashing while handling, after which the event is gone.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Replacing SingleLiveEvent with MutableSharedFlow<Event>() default (no buffer): emit with no subscribers drops silently.
  • Believing Event<T> wrapper with getContentIfNotHandled() solves ordering: it is the same flag idea; works for one consumer only.
  • Treating "navigate" as a command that must run exactly once even after process death.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a Compose snackbar an event or state? → State with a consume handshake; see Q541.
  2. Which approach does Google recommend? → Events as UI state (Q541).
  3. Why not just make the Fragment handle it and skip the ViewModel? → User-initiated actions (click -> navigate) should be handled in UI directly; only business-logic-originated events (result of a network call) need a ViewModel pathway.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "use SharedFlow/Channel instead of SingleLiveEvent". Senior: states the delivery-semantics trade-off (at-most vs at-least once) and picks per event type.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A checkout screen's SingleLiveEvent "show payment error" was consumed by a hidden old fragment instance after a rapid back/forward and the visible one never showed it.

questions.promptHtml: Compare MutableSharedFlow, Channel, and events-as-state for one-off ViewModel-to-UI events. Which would you choose by default and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A comparative, justified decision is the senior signal.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "SharedFlow with replay 0 drops events when no collector exists, e.g. during rotation or while in background. SharedFlow with replay 1 re-delivers after rotation. A Channel buffers events until a collector arrives and delivers each to one consumer, which solves most loss, but it can still lose an event cancelled mid-handling and it's still a stream, which Google now discourages. Events-as-state keeps the event in UI state until the UI acknowledges it, which gives deterministic behavior across config change and process death with saved state. My default is events-as-state; I use a Channel only for fire-and-forget effects where a small loss is acceptable and there is exactly one collector."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SharedFlow(replay=0, extraBuffer=0) SharedFlow(replay=1) Channel(BUFFERED) + receiveAsFlow Event in UiState + ack
No collector at send dropped stored in replay, delivered later buffered (up to 64 default; then send suspends) stored in state
Rotation possibly dropped in the gap replayed -> duplicate delivered once to the new collector persists until acked
Multiple collectors all get it (duplicates) all get it exactly one gets it all see state, ack clears
Background lost if STOPPED replays on START queued, delivered on START queued in state
Process death lost lost lost survives if state saved
Testing Turbine Turbine Turbine assert state
Code complexity low low low medium (ack function)

Chosen by event kind:

  • Navigation/permission/snackbar originating from business logic: state + ack.
  • Pure UI commands from user taps: handle in UI, no ViewModel round trip.
  • Analytics-like fire-and-forget with one consumer: Channel acceptable.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Channel variant
private val _events = Channel<UiEvent>(Channel.BUFFERED)
val events: Flow<UiEvent> = _events.receiveAsFlow()
fun onSave() = viewModelScope.launch { _events.send(UiEvent.Saved) }

// State variant
data class UiState(val pendingEvent: UiEvent? = null)
fun onEventHandled() = _state.update { it.copy(pendingEvent = null) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Channel.UNLIMITED to "never lose events": hides leaks, grows memory if no collector ever arrives.
  • Multiple screens collecting the same Channel: events randomly go to one of them (fan-out).
  • Calling trySend ignoring the result; with a full buffer the event is silently discarded.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. consumeAsFlow vs receiveAsFlow? → consumeAsFlow cancels the channel when the collector is cancelled and can be collected once; receiveAsFlow can be collected repeatedly and leaves the channel open. For ViewModel events, receiveAsFlow.
  2. Is tryEmit on SharedFlow with replay=0 reliable? → Returns false when there are subscribers and the buffer is full; with no subscribers it returns true but discards.
  3. What if two events fire back-to-back with events-as-state? → One slot would overwrite; model pending events as a list/queue, or one-slot per event kind.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior includes a per-case choice, naming exact failure windows (rotation gap, STOPPED) and the process death property.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team using SharedFlow(replay=0) lost "payment succeeded - navigate to receipt" when the user backgrounded the app during a 3DS redirect; the app returned to an unchanged screen.

questions.subtopic: Channel as event bus - where it loses events
questions.promptHtml: You choose Channel.receiveAsFlow() for events. Walk me through every scenario in which an event can still be lost or duplicated.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who copied a pattern from those who understand cancellation and buffering.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "Loss: the collector is cancelled after receive took the element but before the UI handled it, because repeatOnLifecycle cancels at STOPPED; process death; buffer overflow with trySend or DROP_* overflow; consumeAsFlow closing the channel when a collector is cancelled; and ViewModel clear. Duplicate-or-misdirected: two collectors, e.g. two Fragments or a collector launched twice, each get a subset. It's more robust than replay-0 SharedFlow but it's not a guarantee."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Channel.BUFFERED default capacity is 64 (kotlinx.coroutines.channels.defaultBuffer, system property override). send suspends once the buffer is full and the producer coroutine waits. trySend returns ChannelResult.isFailure instead.
  • receiveAsFlow() emits channel.receive() results in a loop. Sequence: receive() returns element -> the flow emit(element) -> collector lambda runs. If the collector coroutine is cancelled between the removal from the channel and the end of handling (cancellation is cooperative, so it takes effect at the next suspension point; if the handler is non-suspending, it finishes), the element is gone. Channel(onUndeliveredElement = {...}) lets you observe/recover such elements, but it fires only for elements not received; documented to run when send/receive was cancelled - for receive-cancelled-after-retrieval treat with care and test.
  • Dispatcher: collecting on Dispatchers.Main.immediate in repeatOnLifecycle means handling is synchronous on main, so a non-suspending handler won't be cancelled mid-way. A suspending handler (e.g. snackbarHostState.showSnackbar) can be.
  • Multiple collectors: Channel is fan-out - each element goes to exactly one receiver. Two collectors after a bug (e.g. collecting in onViewCreated without repeatOnLifecycle, then again after view recreation, not cancelled) -> half the events vanish into the zombie collector.
  • Closing: consumeAsFlow cancels channel on collector cancel -> subsequent send throws CancellationException/ClosedSendChannelException.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Safer collector: handle fast (non-suspending), do heavy work back in the ViewModel
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.events.collect { event ->
            when (event) {
                is UiEvent.Navigate -> findNavController().navigate(event.dest)  // non-suspending
                is UiEvent.ShowToast -> Toast.makeText(ctx, event.msg, Toast.LENGTH_SHORT).show()
            }
        }
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling showSnackbar (suspends until dismissal) inside the channel collector: further events queue behind it; cancel loses the current one.
  • Using Channel.CONFLATED for events: drops all but last.
  • Assuming repeatOnLifecycle(CREATED) avoids the gap; there is still a gap between view destroy and the new view.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How would you make delivery observable? → onUndeliveredElement, plus metrics counting sends vs handled.
  2. Can Channel give exactly once across process death? → No; persist the pending intent (SavedStateHandle or DB).
  3. Why is Dispatchers.Main.immediate relevant? → It lets send from the ViewModel and the collector handling run without extra dispatch, but doesn't remove the cancellation window for suspending handlers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior enumerates cancel-window, fan-out and overflow cases and says when to avoid Channel at all.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Events "randomly" not showing in a two-pane tablet layout: two fragments each collected the same Channel.

questions.promptHtml: What is Google's current guidance on ViewModel-to-UI one-off events, and how would you implement it for a snackbar and for navigation? Where does the guidance hurt?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: They test whether you know the official recommendation and can criticize it with experience.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "The Android architecture docs say ViewModel events should always result in a UI state update; they discourage Channels and other reactive streams for this because delivery is not guaranteed when the producer outlives the consumer. So a snackbar message becomes a nullable field in UiState; the UI shows it, then calls viewModel.messageShown() to clear it. Navigation triggered by business logic works the same: a navigateTo field consumed after navigating. The costs: ack boilerplate, one-slot overwrites, risk of showing twice if the UI is torn down before the ack, and awkwardness when the navigation back stack keeps the screen alive."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Premise: UI state is a faithful description of the screen at every instant. A pending message is part of that description until it's displayed.
  • Benefits: reproducible after rotation, back-stack return, and (with SavedStateHandle) process death; easy to unit test (assert state); no lost events when backgrounded.
  • Consumption protocol, at-least-once: show -> ack. Can duplicate if the process or composition dies between show and ack.
  • Choose at-most-once by acking before showing (read message, call messageShown(), then display); choose at-least-once by acking after. Pick per importance: payment confirmation = at-least-once; "Saved" toast = at-most-once.
  • Multiple pending events: List<UiMessage> with ids; ack removes by id.
  • Navigation: after calling navController.navigate(...) the screen is typically not on top; if it stays on the back stack and the flag isn't cleared, popping back re-navigates. Always ack right after navigating.
  • Criticism: pure-state purists vs practitioners: commands are not state; but the ack handshake gives correctness at the cost of ceremony.
  • Compose snippet in Google docs uses LaunchedEffect(userMessage) keyed on the message.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
data class UiMessage(val id: Long, val text: String)
data class UiState(val messages: List<UiMessage> = emptyList(), val navigateTo: Route? = null)

fun onError(text: String) = _state.update { it.copy(messages = it.messages + UiMessage(nextId++, text)) }
fun messageShown(id: Long) = _state.update { s -> s.copy(messages = s.messages.filterNot { it.id == id }) }
fun navigated() = _state.update { it.copy(navigateTo = null) }

// Compose
state.messages.firstOrNull()?.let { m ->
    LaunchedEffect(m.id) {
        vm.messageShown(m.id)            // ack-before-show: at-most-once
        snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(m.text)
    }
}
state.navigateTo?.let { route -> LaunchedEffect(route) { nav.navigate(route); vm.navigated() } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Forgetting to clear the field: re-fires on every recomposition-restart or rotation.
  • Using state-with-ack for rapid-fire events (typing haptics); use UI-local handling.
  • Storing a Context-dependent string resource in state instead of a resource id/UiText.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does an event from a click belong? → Handle in the UI layer; no ViewModel round trip unless business logic decides the outcome.
  2. How do you survive process death? → Keep pending-event in SavedStateHandle (serializable) or recompute from persisted data.
  3. Ack-before vs ack-after: which? → Depends on the cost of losing vs duplicating.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE repeats "use state". Senior defines the ack protocol, at-most vs at-least once, queue vs slot, and the back-stack navigation gotcha.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Team adopted state-based navigation; after pressing back, the screen re-navigated forward because navigateTo had not been cleared on a fast pop.

questions.contextHtml:
A shopping cart screen was migrated from LiveData to StateFlow. QA reports: adding an item does nothing visually until the user rotates the device; then the item is there. Crash rate is flat (0.2%). Code:

class CartViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _items = MutableStateFlow(mutableListOf<CartItem>())
    val items: StateFlow<List<CartItem>> = _items

    fun add(item: CartItem) {
        _items.value.add(item)
        _items.value = _items.value
    }
    fun remove(id: Long) { _items.value.removeAll { it.id == id } }
}

The RecyclerView adapter is a ListAdapter with DiffUtil. Product also says "it worked with LiveData postValue(list)".
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s), explain why it worked with LiveData, and fix it properly.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Call notifyDataSetChanged" or "use postValue". Misses that StateFlow compares by equals, that the same instance is equal to itself, and that ListAdapter.submitList ignores the same list instance.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the adapter use ListAdapter/DiffUtil (yes)? Is the list ever mutated off main thread (concurrent modification risk)? Did the LiveData version create a new list per update? Is state saved anywhere?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Hotfix: _items.value = _items.value + item and _items.value.filterNot {} using immutable copies.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) StateFlow ignores assignment of an equal value: the same instance == itself -> no emission. (b) Even if it emitted, ListAdapter.submitList(sameInstance) returns early, so no diff. (c) remove mutates in place and never assigns at all. (d) Red herring: DiffUtil areItemsTheSame.
  4. How I'd verify each: Unit test with Turbine: vm.items.test { awaitItem(); vm.add(x); expectNoEvents() } demonstrates no emission. Debug: log identity hash codes of the list on assignment. Check ListAdapter.submitList source (if (newList == mList) return).
  5. Root cause: The state holder holds a mutable list whose identity never changes. MutableStateFlow.value = x uses equals; list == list is true for the same instance, so no collector is notified. The rotation "fixes" it because a new collector reads the current value, which already contains the mutation. LiveData setValue(sameList) always dispatched, hiding the problem; and the adapter, being passed the same instance... in the LiveData version the adapter likely received a copy (toList()) at some point.
  6. Fix: Short-term: immutable updates with update:
private val _items = MutableStateFlow<List<CartItem>>(emptyList())
val items: StateFlow<List<CartItem>> = _items.asStateFlow()
fun add(item: CartItem) = _items.update { it + item }
fun remove(id: Long) = _items.update { list -> list.filterNot { it.id == id } }

Long-term: UiState as an immutable data class, ImmutableList/persistentListOf from kotlinx.collections.immutable for Compose stability, and exposing List (read-only interface) is not a guarantee, so never cast. 7. Prevention: Detekt/lint rule: no MutableStateFlow<Mutable*>; code review item; unit tests asserting emission; update {} over .value =. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not value = value.toMutableList().apply{...} scattered around (verbose, easy to forget). Not forcing re-emission with a version counter hack. Copying is O(n) per update: for 10k-item lists use persistent collections or paging.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if two coroutines call add simultaneously? → Old code loses updates (and may throw ConcurrentModificationException); update {} is a CAS loop, so both are applied; keep the lambda pure because it can run more than once.
  • Would a data class CartState(val items: MutableList<..>) + copy() work? → copy() creates a new wrapper but if items is the same list, equals compares the same list instance -> equal -> no emit.
  • Is the exposed StateFlow<List> safe? → Read-only by type; a downcast could mutate; use immutable collections for hard guarantees.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "favorites" toggle flickered back after rotation across the whole app; a shared mutable list lived in a singleton repository's StateFlow, mutated from three screens, and each screen saw different staleness. Switching to immutable copies fixed all three.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests notifyDataSetChanged or postValue; cannot explain why no emission.
  • Hire: Explains equality-based dedupe, fixes with immutable copy and update.
  • Strong hire: Also explains ListAdapter early-return, lost-update race, persistent collections/Compose stability, and adds a regression test plus a lint rule.

questions.contextHtml:
Login screen, 1.2M DAU, 60% on Android 12+. After release 8.4, support tickets: "after logging in the home screen opens twice - I have to press back twice" (about 1.5% of logins) and "login succeeds but nothing happens" (about 0.4%). Crash rate unchanged. Code in 8.4 (changed from SingleLiveEvent):

class LoginViewModel : ViewModel() {
    private val _nav = MutableSharedFlow<NavEvent>(replay = 1)
    val nav = _nav.asSharedFlow()
    fun onLoginSuccess() { viewModelScope.launch { _nav.emit(NavEvent.Home) } }
}
// Fragment.onViewCreated:
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewModel.nav.collect { findNavController().navigate(R.id.action_login_to_home) }
}

Duplicates correlate with rotation or returning from background shortly after login. The "nothing happens" cases correlate with users who tapped login and then locked the screen.
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose both symptoms, ship a fix, and say what you would standardize across the codebase.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use distinctUntilChanged" or "set replay to 0" without explaining the loss window; or blames Navigation component.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the ViewModel scoped to the Fragment or Activity/nav graph (if graph-scoped it survives navigating away and back)? Does the back stack keep LoginFragment after navigating (popUpTo)? Any repeatOnLifecycle? Is the same flow collected elsewhere? Did SingleLiveEvent previously mask this?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Server-side remote flag to ship fix fast; hotfix: guard navigate with currentDestination?.id == R.id.loginFragment, which stops double navigation within the hour.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) replay = 1 replays the last NavEvent.Home to every new collector: after rotation, the new view collects and re-navigates. (b) Collector uses lifecycleScope of the view without repeatOnLifecycle: while STOPPED, navigate is attempted and can fail or navigate while the FragmentManager state is saved. (c) "Nothing happens": with locked screen, the event is emitted while no collector is actively handling (view destroyed/stopped); with replay=1 on resume it should replay... unless the ViewModel was recreated. (d) Red herring: server-side double login responses.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce with "Don't keep activities" + rotation; log subscriber count (nav.subscriptionCount); check NavController back stack via adb shell dumpsys activity top; Crashlytics custom keys for currentDestination; Turbine test: emit then re-collect shows replay.
  5. Root cause: replay=1 made the event sticky, the exact bug SingleLiveEvent was invented to avoid. For "nothing happens": the LoginFragment collector lacked lifecycle scoping, so during the STOPPED phase the navigate call threw/was swallowed (navigating after onSaveInstanceState is ignored by the nav component in some flows) and the event was consumed from the stream; a replay=1 cache held it but the next collection after a real recreation of the ViewModel (process death while locked) was gone.
  6. Fix: Short-term: guard + resetReplayCache() after handling is racy (don't). Real fix: model as state with ack:
data class LoginUiState(val loggedIn: Boolean = false)
fun onNavigated() = _state.update { it.copy(loggedIn = false) }

viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.state.map { it.loggedIn }.distinctUntilChanged().filter { it }.collect {
            findNavController().navigate(R.id.action_login_to_home)
            viewModel.onNavigated()
        }
    }
}

Better: after login, persist session in the repository and let an auth-state-driven root navigation decide; no event at all. Long-term: shared NavigationState conventions. 7. Prevention: Lint/Detekt rule flagging MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1) named event; instrumentation test with ActivityScenario.recreate() after emit; review checklist: "what happens on rotation / background / process death?". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not replay=0 alone (loses on lock screen). Not Channel as a silent fix without checking process death. Not a global Event<T> wrapper (single-consumer flag, same SingleLiveEvent flaws).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if navigation must survive process death? → Derive the destination from persisted auth state at start; do not carry a transient event.
  • How does Navigation Compose change this? → Same; hoist state, call navController.navigate in LaunchedEffect(state.navigateTo) and ack.
  • Multiple screens react to login? → Event is no longer one-consumer: that's a signal it's state (session) not an event.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "welcome back" navigation event replayed on every rotation for a month because someone "fixed" lost events by setting replay=1; the real cause was a collector with no lifecycle scoping. We moved to auth-state-driven navigation and deleted the event entirely.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot connect replay=1 to rotation duplicates; guesses at server causes.
  • Hire: Identifies replay stickiness and missing lifecycle scope; fixes with state+ack or Channel.
  • Strong hire: Also reasons about loss windows, process death, ViewModel scope, auth-state-driven navigation, regression test with recreate, and rollout/monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
A Compose screen shows an error snackbar using events-as-state per Google's guidance. Users on slow devices report the same "Could not sync" snackbar appearing a second time after rotating the phone while it was showing, and about 2% of sessions show it again after returning from a deep link screen. Code:

@Composable
fun SyncScreen(vm: SyncViewModel, snackbar: SnackbarHostState) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    state.userMessage?.let { msg ->
        LaunchedEffect(msg) {
            snackbar.showSnackbar(msg)
            vm.userMessageShown()
        }
    }
}
fun userMessageShown() { _state.update { it.copy(userMessage = null) } }

The user message is a plain String. Two sync failures in a row produce the identical text.
questions.promptHtml: Why is it shown twice and why are consecutive identical failures sometimes not shown at all? Fix it.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add remember" or "use a Toast". Doesn't realize showSnackbar suspends until dismissal and is cancelled by recomposition teardown.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Snackbar duration (Short=4s/Long=10s/Indefinite)? Does SnackbarHostState live in rememberSaveable or the Scaffold? Is the message lost on process death? Are failures retried automatically?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ack before showing, which turns it into at-most-once and stops duplicates; ship as hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) showSnackbar suspends until dismissed; on rotation the composition is disposed, the LaunchedEffect is cancelled with CancellationException, userMessageShown() never runs, state still has the message, new composition shows it again. (b) Consecutive identical strings: userMessage = "Could not sync" set while the old one is still non-null yields equal state: StateFlow dedupes, LaunchedEffect(msg) key unchanged, so the second failure never shows. (c) Deep-link return: composition for the screen was removed and re-added with a still-pending message (never acked because dismissal cancelled the effect). (d) Red herring: duration or SnackbarHost recomposition.
  4. How I'd verify each: Compose UI test with ComposeTestRule.activityRule.scenario.recreate() while the snackbar is visible; Turbine on state to confirm no emission for equal messages; logs around userMessageShown.
  5. Root cause: Ack placed after a suspension point that can be cancelled by composition lifecycle; messages identified by value rather than identity.
  6. Fix:
data class UserMessage(val id: Long, val text: String)
// vm
fun onSyncFailed() = _state.update { it.copy(messages = it.messages + UserMessage(nextId++, "Could not sync")) }
fun messageShown(id: Long) = _state.update { s -> s.copy(messages = s.messages.filterNot { it.id == id }) }

state.messages.firstOrNull()?.let { m ->
    LaunchedEffect(m.id) {
        vm.messageShown(m.id)          // consume first -> at-most-once; rotation can't redisplay
        snackbar.showSnackbar(m.text)
    }
}

If the message is critical (must be seen), keep ack-after but guard with try/finally? No: finally would ack on rotation too (cancellation), defeating the point; instead ack only on SnackbarResult returned normally: val r = snackbar.showSnackbar(...) completes only when dismissed; a rotation cancels it. That's at-least-once, duplicates on rotation acceptable for critical messages. 7. Prevention: Compose test with recreate(); id-based messages as convention; shared UserMessageHost composable so each screen doesn't reimplement. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not delay hacks; not a SharedFlow just for snackbars (loss in background); at-most-once means a rotation during the first second can drop the message: acceptable for "Could not sync", not for "Payment failed".

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the message is a string resource with args? → Store UiText (resource id + args) not a resolved String, so locale changes work.
  • Two messages queue up? → Queue in state; show first, ack, next recomposes with the next id.
  • Process death? → Persist critical messages (SavedStateHandle) or re-derive from data (e.g. "last sync failed" from DB).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "Saved" snackbar kept re-appearing for every list item edited; the effect key was a constant Unit so the old message stuck and new equal ones deduped. Message ids ended the argument.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Cannot explain double show; suggests removing StateFlow.
  • Hire: Understands cancellation of LaunchedEffect skips the ack, uses ack-before or ids.
  • Strong hire: Discusses at-most vs at-least once per message importance, StateFlow dedupe of equal values, UiText, queueing, recreate tests.

questions.contextHtml:
Release 5.2 migrated the Orders screen from LiveData to StateFlow (staged rollout 20% -> 100%). Crashlytics now shows a new top crash on the migrated screen, 0.9% of sessions, 70% on Android 13+:

java.lang.IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState
    at androidx.fragment.app.FragmentManager.checkStateLoss
    at androidx.fragment.app.DialogFragment.show
    at OrdersFragment$onViewCreated$1.invokeSuspend(OrdersFragment.kt:58)

Battery dashboard also shows 2x background network calls on that screen. Code:

override fun onViewCreated(v: View, s: Bundle?) {
    lifecycleScope.launch {
        viewModel.state.collect { render(it) }   // render() may show a ConfirmDialog
    }
}
// ViewModel
val state = repo.orders().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.Eagerly, OrdersState.Loading)

Before the migration it was viewModel.state.observe(viewLifecycleOwner) { render(it) }.
questions.promptHtml: Explain both symptoms, how you'd roll back/mitigate, and the permanent fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Wrap the dialog in a try/catch" or "use commitAllowingStateLoss". Treats the symptom, misses that the collector ignores lifecycle and the upstream never stops.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is repo.orders() a polling flow? What does render do with dialogs? Fragment's lifecycleScope or viewLifecycleOwner? Does the crash occur when the app is backgrounded (state saved)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Halt the staged rollout at current percentage; use the remote kill switch (feature flag) for the new path if present; ship a hotfix to the collector.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) lifecycleScope of the Fragment (not view) with plain collect keeps collecting in STOPPED; a state emission arrives after onSaveInstanceState and render shows a DialogFragment -> exception. (b) SharingStarted.Eagerly keeps the upstream polling in background -> 2x network and wakeups. (c) Collection launched in onViewCreated with the Fragment's lifecycle outlives the view and leaks across view re-creation (stale binding). (d) Red herring: Android 13 specific behavior; it's just the user base.
