  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce: put the app in background during a refresh; check adb shell dumpsys activity for fragment state; Profiler network trace in background; log lifecycle.currentState in collect; LeakCanary for leaked views.
  5. Root cause: LiveData's observe(viewLifecycleOwner) implicitly paused delivery below STARTED and removed on view destroy. The migration dropped that, plus the upstream strategy changed from liveData {}/asLiveData (5 s timeout, stops when inactive) to Eagerly (never stops).
  6. Fix:
viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch {
    viewLifecycleOwner.repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED) {
        viewModel.state.collect(::render)
    }
}
val state = repo.orders().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), OrdersState.Loading)

Also convert the dialog showing to state-based events with ack (Q541) so a re-render doesn't show a dialog repeatedly; shared collectWhenStarted extension for all screens. 7. Prevention: Lint/Detekt rule for lifecycleScope.launch { ...collect } in Fragments; migration checklist with the 3 equivalences (lifecycle, sharing strategy, dedupe); a test with LifecycleRegistry moving to STOPPED asserting no collection; battery/background-network metric as a rollout gate. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not commitAllowingStateLoss (hides lost UI state). Not launchWhenStarted (deprecated; pauses but doesn't cancel the upstream). 5_000 ms keeps upstream alive over config changes but costs 5 s of background work on every stop.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not Lazily? → Starts at first subscriber but never stops, same battery issue.
  • Does repeatOnLifecycle refetch on every restart? → Re-collects; with WhileSubscribed and 5 s expired, upstream restarts and re-queries; that's often desirable (fresh data).
  • What if we need the data to continue syncing in background? → Move that to WorkManager/repository scope, not UI-driven collection.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A staged rollout caught the issue at 20%, which is why we gate migrations behind a flag and watch background wakeups, not just crash-free rate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Suggests try/catch or allowing state loss.
  • Hire: Identifies missing lifecycle scoping, uses repeatOnLifecycle and WhileSubscribed.
  • Strong hire: Also explains upstream behavior change vs asLiveData, rollout gating, dialog-as-state, lint rule and tests.

questions.promptHtml: How do LiveData and StateFlow differ in when their upstream work starts and stops, and what leaks can each cause?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Shows understanding of hot vs lifecycle-bound sources and resource usage.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: "A MutableLiveData/MutableStateFlow itself has no upstream; the question is about derived ones. liveData {}/asLiveData start when the first observer is active (onActive) and cancel 5 seconds after the last one goes inactive. stateIn takes a SharingStarted policy: Eagerly/Lazily never stop, WhileSubscribed(5_000) mirrors the LiveData behavior. Leaks: observeForever that's never removed; a StateFlow collector in a scope that outlives the UI; a ViewModel holding a Fragment/Context reference in a lambda; a hot upstream kept alive by Eagerly."

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• LiveData.observe(owner, ...) is leak-safe: removed on DESTROYED. observeForever isn't; you must removeObserver.
  • onActive/onInactive in MediatorLiveData and custom LiveData (e.g. location) register/unregister sources when the first/last active observer comes/goes. This is why LiveData wrappers around callbacks (sensors, location) were idiomatic.
  • Flow equivalents: callbackFlow + awaitClose (the unregistration) behind stateIn(WhileSubscribed). Without awaitClose, the callback leaks.
  • stateIn(viewModelScope, WhileSubscribed(stopTimeoutMillis = 5_000)): subscriptionCount goes 0 -> after 5 s the upstream is cancelled; resubscribing restarts it. 5 s covers config change (~ a few hundred ms) with margin.
  • Scope pitfalls: collecting the ViewModel's StateFlow with GlobalScope or an app scope; viewModelScope is cancelled in onCleared, which stops stateIn.
  • Config change: ViewModel and its StateFlow survive; the collector is cancelled and a new one subscribes; with 5 s timeout upstream not restarted.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// custom lifecycle-bound LiveData
class LocationLiveData(private val client: Client) : LiveData<Loc>() {
    override fun onActive() = client.start(::setValue)
    override fun onInactive() = client.stop()
}
// Flow equivalent
fun Client.locations(): Flow<Loc> = callbackFlow {
    val cb = { l: Loc -> trySend(l) }
    start(cb)
    awaitClose { stop() }
}
val loc = client.locations().stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), null)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Eagerly for GPS/sensor/websocket flows.
  • Forgetting that WhileSubscribed only counts collectors on that StateFlow; a second collector in a background service would keep it alive.
  • observeForever in a ViewModel without removing it in onCleared.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I observe subscriptionCount? → MutableSharedFlow.subscriptionCount (StateFlow<Int>); also available on StateFlow via stateIn-produced SharedFlow.
  2. Why 5_000? → Android's ANR threshold is 5 s for input events; for config change the practical reason is covering recreation; also matches asLiveData default.
  3. Does stateIn initial value get re-emitted after restart? → The last value stays in the StateFlow (use replayExpirationMillis if you want reset behavior with shareIn; for stateIn the value remains).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Senior maps onActive/onInactive to WhileSubscribed, mentions awaitClose, and flags observeForever and Eagerly as the usual leak sources.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Battery regression where a location StateFlow with Eagerly kept the GPS on from app start until process death.

questions.contextHtml: You join a 25-engineer team, 60 screens. Event handling is inconsistent: 20 screens use SingleLiveEvent, 15 use MutableSharedFlow<Event>(), 10 use Channel, 15 are Compose with ad-hoc mutableStateOf flags. Last quarter produced 3 incidents: duplicate order submissions after rotation, a missing "session expired" dialog after a background-to-foreground transition, and a double snackbar. The tech lead wants a single standard and a migration plan with no feature freeze. Roadmap: Compose migration over the next 3 quarters.
questions.promptHtml: What standard do you propose, how do you roll it out, and how do you decide exceptions?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Everyone use SharedFlow" or "rewrite all at once". No classification of events, no rollout or measurement.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What events exist (navigation, messages, permission requests, one-time effects)? Which must survive process death (payments, auth expiry)? View or Compose in new screens? Is there a UDF base class? Test coverage per screen?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the 3 incidents locally (ack-before for snackbar, state for session-expired, idempotency key for order submit) without waiting for the standard.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (causes of inconsistency): no guideline; copy-paste patterns; no lint; each approach has different failure windows that nobody documented.
  4. How I'd verify: Audit via grep of event types; classify each event by criticality; write a recreate/background test harness to reproduce the 3 incidents; measure after rollout with Crashlytics and custom logs.
  5. Root cause: We have one problem (delivery semantics across producer/consumer lifetimes) solved five different ways with different guarantees.
  6. Fix (proposal): A decision table:
Event kind                                  Mechanism
click -> navigate/show (UI knows outcome)  handle in UI, no ViewModel round trip
business result -> UI feedback (snackbar)   events-as-state, id-based message list, ack-before-show
business result -> navigation               state field + ack after navigate, or derive from state (auth)
critical (payment, session expired)         state persisted in repository/SavedStateHandle; at-least-once
high-rate fire-and-forget, single consumer  Channel(BUFFERED) + receiveAsFlow in repeatOnLifecycle
SharedFlow as event bus                     banned in ViewModel->UI

Provide a tiny shared library: UiMessage, MessageHost composable/collectMessages extension, a base UiState interface with messages, and tests utilities. For order submission also add an idempotency key; events can duplicate, so server must tolerate duplicates. 7. Prevention: Lint/Detekt rules (no MutableSharedFlow in ViewModel classes exposing event types, no SingleLiveEvent), PR template item ("what happens on rotation/background/process death?"), a sample module, and screens migrated opportunistically when touched, plus a tracked burndown. Compose screens use the standard from day one. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a big-bang rewrite; legacy SingleLiveEvent screens remain until touched. Not one mechanism for everything: Channel stays legal for narrow cases. The standard costs boilerplate (ack functions), mitigated by the shared helpers. I'd not claim "exactly once": it is not achievable; I'd design for idempotency.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Engineers push back on ack boilerplate. → Show the incidents, provide helpers/templates, and make the default path two lines in the screen.
  • A screen needs to show the same event on two panes. → That's state; both panes render it, either acks.
  • KMP shared ViewModels later? → State+ack is pure Kotlin, so it ports; Channel works too; LiveData/SingleLiveEvent don't.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: We tried to ban Channel outright and engineers moved events into overloaded boolean flags. A decision table with explicit exceptions got adopted because it admitted that events differ.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: Picks one mechanism for all with no justification; no migration plan.
  • Hire: Classifies events, chooses state+ack as default, proposes incremental migration and lint.
  • Strong hire: Adds delivery-semantics reasoning, idempotency for critical flows, process-death handling, shared tooling, adoption strategy, and metrics.
